blocks.text: Rockets move by expelling burning gas through engines at their rear. The ignited fuel turns into a high-pressure gas which is expelled with extremely high velocity from the rocket engines (Fig. 2.18). The rocket gains momentum equal to the momentum of the gas expelled from the engine but in the opposite direction. The rocket engines continue to expel gases after the rocket has begun moving, so the rocket continues to gain more and more momentum; instead of travelling at a steady speed it gets faster and faster so long as the engines are operating. Fuel and oxygen mix in the combustion chamber, hot gases exhaust the chamber at very high velocity, the gain in momentum of the gases equals the gain in momentum of the rocket, and the gas and rocket push against each other and move in opposite directions.

blocks.alt: Cut-away rocket, top to bottom: nose cone, payload, a blue tank of liquid hydrogen fuel, a green tank of liquid oxygen, pumps and pipes, the combustion chamber and the nozzle. Hot gases rush out of the nozzle downward and a red arrow shows the thrust pushing the rocket upward.
blocks.caption: Cut-away rocket: fuel (liquid hydrogen), liquid oxygen and combustion chamber (original diagram after Figure 2.18).

blocks.text: A rocket carries its own fuel, in the form of liquid or solid hydrogen and oxygen, so it can work at great heights where very little or no air is present. To provide enough upward thrust to overcome gravity, a typical rocket consumes about 10 000 kg s^-1 of fuel and ejects the burnt gases at speeds of over 4000 m s^-1; in fact more than 80% of the launch mass of a rocket consists of fuel. One way to overcome the problem of the mass of fuel is to make the rocket from several rockets linked together: when one rocket has done its job it is discarded, leaving the others to carry the spacecraft further up at ever greater speed.

blocks.title: Acceleration of a rocket
blocks.text: If m is the mass of the gases ejected per second with velocity v relative to the rocket, the change in momentum per second of the ejected gases is mv. This equals the thrust produced by the engine on the body of the rocket, so the acceleration a of the rocket is a = mv/M ... (2.42, as printed), where M is the mass of the rocket. As the fuel is burned and ejected the mass M of the rocket decreases, and hence the acceleration increases.

blocks.prompt: A rocket of mass 2.0 x 10^5 kg ejects gas at 5.0 x 10^3 kg s^-1 with a speed of 4000 m s^-1 relative to the rocket. Find the thrust and the initial acceleration, and say what happens to the acceleration as fuel burns.
blocks.explanation: Thrust = mv = 5.0 x 10^3 kg s^-1 x 4000 m s^-1 = 2.0 x 10^7 N; a = mv/M = 2.0 x 10^7 N / 2.0 x 10^5 kg = 100 m s^-2 (ignoring gravity; with gravity the net upward acceleration is about 90 m s^-2). As fuel is ejected M decreases while mv stays the same, so the acceleration increases.

items: A rocket gains momentum equal and opposite to the expelled gas; it keeps accelerating while the engines run. It carries hydrogen and oxygen, burns about 10 000 kg s^-1, exhausts at over 4000 m s^-1, is over 80% fuel, and is built in stages.
a = mv/M: m = mass ejected per second, v = gas velocity relative to the rocket, mv = thrust, M = rocket mass (falls as fuel burns, so a rises).
